source_evidence: Each class of shares of the mutual fund invests in the same "pool" (or investment portfolio) of securities, but each class may have different fees and expenses.
answer:
Mutual fund classes are different types of shares offered by the same fund. They invest in the same portfolio, but their fees and expenses can differ, which can lead to different investment returns over time.

For example, Class A shares might charge a fee when you buy them, while Class C shares might charge ongoing fees and a fee when you sell within a specified period. No-load classes do not charge a sales load, but they can still have ongoing expenses or transaction fees. Institutional shares may have relatively low ongoing expenses, but access or minimum investment requirements can vary.

When comparing classes, consider all costs—not just the fee charged at purchase—including ongoing expenses and any fees that may apply when selling. The class with the lowest initial cost may not have the lowest costs over time.
